units.title: Unit 23 — Shopping
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 23. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify common objects and places in a supermarket and describe how products are displayed.
Understand how special offers, product placement and queues influence shopping decisions.
Use practical shopping phrases for returning purchases, replacing products and requesting refunds.
Compare shopping centres with street markets using appropriate descriptions and expressions.
Recognise word stress and use phrases such as under one roof, a wide range of and haggle over a price.

items.example: The supermarket closes at nine on weekdays.
items.note: A large shop that sells food and household products.

items.example: The children chose some sweets for the journey.
items.note: British English: sweets; American English often uses candy.

items.example: I picked up a basket because I only needed a few things.
items.note: A small container carried by shoppers.

items.example: We used a trolley for our weekly shopping.
items.note: A wheeled cart for carrying shopping; British English.

items.example: I found the flour on the bottom shelf.
items.note: Singular noun; plural: shelves.

items.example: The biscuits are on the middle shelves.
items.note: Irregular plural of shelf: shelf → shelves.

items.pt: caixa do supermercado; local de pagamento
items.example: There were only two people at the checkout.
items.note: The place where you pay for your shopping.

items.example: Shoppers were waiting for the doors to open.
items.note: A person buying things in a shop.

items.example: I try not to spend money on things I do not need.
items.note: Spend money on something; past tense: spent.

items.pt: fazer alguém fazer algo; levar alguém a fazer algo
items.example: Bright displays can make shoppers buy more food.
items.note: Causative pattern: make + person + base verb, without to.

items.example: They sell fresh bread every morning.
items.note: Food that has recently been prepared or has not been stored for long.

items.example: The baskets are beside the entrance.
items.note: Noun for the place where people enter; stress the first syllable.

items.example: The staff rearranged the shelves last night.
items.note: Arrange again, especially in a different order or position.

items.example: I bought a small bar of chocolate after lunch.
items.note: Bar is used for one long, solid piece of chocolate.

items.example: A long queue formed near the tills.
items.note: British English noun meaning a line of people waiting.

items.example: We waited in a queue for ten minutes.
items.note: In British English, you can also queue for something.

items.example: Those imported biscuits are too expensive.
items.note: Opposite: cheap; use more expensive for comparison.

items.example: The receipt lists every item we bought.
items.note: One individual thing in a group of products.

items.pt: ter probabilidade de fazer algo; provavelmente fazer algo
items.example: People are more likely to buy food when they are hungry.
items.note: Be likely to + base verb expresses probability.

items.example: There is a special offer on coffee this week.
items.note: A temporary reduction or deal on the usual price.

items.word: three for the price of two
items.pt: leve três pelo preço de dois
items.example: The shop sells three yoghurts for the price of two.
items.note: A promotion where three products cost the same as two.

items.example: Please do not throw the leftovers away.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: throw it away, not throw away it.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: We met outside the shopping centre.
items.note: British English spelling: centre; a building or area containing many shops.

items.pt: feira de rua; mercado de rua
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The street market sells vegetables and second-hand books.
items.note: An outdoor market with separate stalls.

items.pt: no mesmo lugar; sob o mesmo teto
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: This shopping centre has dozens of shops under one roof.
items.note: Describes services or activities available in one building or place.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: Online shopping is convenient when you are busy.
items.note: Useful because it saves time or effort; not necessarily pleasant.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The market offers a wide range of fresh produce.
items.note: A variety of different things in the same general category.

items.pt: algo errado com alguma coisa; algum defeito em algo
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: There is something wrong with the headphones I bought.
items.note: Use there is something wrong with + item for a problem or fault.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The shop agreed to replace the broken kettle.
items.note: Give a new or different item instead of the original.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: They gave me a full refund for the faulty jacket.
items.note: A noun for money returned after a purchase; the verb refund has different stress.

items.pt: receber um reembolso; obter devolução do dinheiro
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: You can get a refund if you keep the receipt.
items.note: Common shopping phrase; also ask for a refund.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The market has a lively atmosphere on Saturdays.
items.note: The general feeling or mood of a place.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: A farmer sold apples from a small stall.
items.note: A stand or small selling area in a market.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: Visitors sometimes haggle at the street market.
items.note: Try to agree a lower price instead of accepting the first one.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: They haggled over the price of an old table.
items.note: Common pattern: haggle over a price or haggle with a seller.

items.pt: devolver algo à loja; levar algo de volta
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: I took the jacket back because it was too small.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb; when shopping, it often means return a purchase.

items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The seller agreed to a lower price.
items.note: Lower is the comparative of low in this expression.

items.pt: compre um e leve outro grátis
items.section: B · Shopping centres and street markets
items.example: The bakery has a buy one, get one free offer today.
items.note: A promotion offering a second item without extra charge.

units.title: Unit 24 — Food
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 24. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Name common fruits, vegetables, salad ingredients, meats, fish and seafood.
Recognise British food terms such as aubergine, courgette and prawns.
Distinguish animals from the names of their meat, especially cow/beef, calf/veal and pig/pork.
Describe common ingredients of mixed salads and salad dressings.
Use everyday food vocabulary accurately, including a bunch of grapes, vegetarian and the skin of fruit.

items.example: Fresh fruit is available at the market.
items.note: Often uncountable as a general food category; fruits can mean different kinds.

items.example: We cut the pineapple into small pieces.
items.note: A tropical fruit with thick, rough skin.

items.example: This peach is sweet and juicy.
items.note: A soft fruit with a stone in the centre.

items.example: She put a strawberry on each slice of cake.
items.note: Plural: strawberries.

items.example: I often take grapes to work as a snack.
items.note: Grapes grow in groups called bunches.

items.example: He bought a bunch of grapes for the picnic.
items.note: Bunch is the usual collective noun for a group of grapes.

items.example: We added black olives to the salad.
items.note: Often eaten in salads or as a snack.

items.example: I ate a pear after lunch.
items.note: The fruit; do not confuse it with pair, which sounds the same.

items.example: We served cold melon for dessert.
items.note: A large, round fruit with soft flesh.

items.example: Squeeze a little lemon over the fish.
items.note: In Brazilian Portuguese, this is commonly distinguished from green lime.

items.example: The sauce has coconut in it.
items.note: A tropical fruit with a hard shell.

items.example: We buy fresh vegetables twice a week.
items.note: A broad food category including many edible plants.

items.example: I cooked some green beans with garlic.
items.note: The book illustrates green beans; the word can also refer to dried beans.

items.example: We added peas to the rice.
items.note: Small round green vegetables; singular: pea.

items.example: Chop an onion before heating the oil.
items.note: Common aromatic vegetable used in savoury dishes.

items.example: I added two cloves of garlic to the sauce.
items.note: Usually uncountable as an ingredient; a clove is one segment.

items.example: She grated a carrot for the salad.
items.note: A usually orange root vegetable.

items.example: We fried some mushrooms with onions.
items.note: Edible fungi used in many dishes.

items.example: Roasted aubergine tastes good with garlic.
items.note: British English; American English: eggplant.

items.example: Slice the courgette and cook it in a little oil.
items.note: British English; American English: zucchini.

items.example: She used a red pepper in the salad.
items.note: Here pepper means sweet/bell pepper, not ground black pepper.

items.example: They served cooked cabbage with potatoes.
items.note: A leafy vegetable; it can be eaten raw or cooked.

items.example: Steam the broccoli for a few minutes.
items.note: Usually uncountable when naming the vegetable.

items.example: Fresh spinach is good in salads and soups.
items.note: A leafy green vegetable; normally uncountable.

items.example: We had a simple salad with dinner.
items.note: Often a mixture of vegetables, many of them uncooked.

items.example: Use uncooked vegetables for this salad.
items.note: Food that has not been cooked; raw is a common synonym.

items.example: Check the ingredients before you start cooking.
items.note: One of the foods or substances used to make a dish.

items.example: Wash the lettuce before making the salad.
items.note: A leafy vegetable that is usually eaten raw.

items.example: I put two tomatoes in the salad.
items.note: British pronunciation; plural: tomatoes.

items.example: Cut the cucumber into thin slices.
items.note: A fresh vegetable often eaten uncooked.

items.example: This salad dressing contains olive oil and lemon.
items.note: A sauce added to salad, often made using oil and vinegar or lemon.

items.example: Pour a little oil into the pan.
items.note: Usually uncountable; olive oil is common in salad dressing.

items.example: Add a spoonful of vinegar to the dressing.
items.note: An acidic liquid often mixed with oil for salads.

items.example: We ordered a mixed salad to share.
items.note: A salad containing several different ingredients.

items.example: A green salad goes well with grilled fish.
items.note: A salad mainly made with green leaves and vegetables.

items.example: We do not eat much meat during the week.
items.note: Food from animals such as cows, pigs and sheep. Usually uncountable.

items.example: We often cook fish with lemon and herbs.
items.note: Fish is normally both singular and plural; it may mean the animal or the food.

items.example: The cow was grazing in the field.
items.note: The animal; its meat is called beef.

items.example: The calf stayed close to its mother.
items.note: A young cow; its meat is called veal. Plural: calves.

items.example: Several sheep were standing near the gate.
items.note: The animal; a young sheep is a lamb. Sheep is also the plural.

items.example: A lamb followed the flock across the field.
items.note: A young sheep; compare with lamb meaning its meat.

items.example: The farmer keeps pigs in a large field.
items.note: The animal; its meat is usually called pork.

items.example: A chicken walked around the farmyard.
items.note: The bird; a hen is specifically an adult female chicken.

items.example: The hen laid an egg this morning.
items.note: A female adult chicken.

items.example: They cooked beef with onions and carrots.
items.note: The meat from a cow or other cattle.

items.pt: carne de vitela; carne de bezerro
items.example: Veal is not common on the menu here.
items.note: Meat from a calf, a young cow.

items.example: Roast lamb is often served with vegetables.
items.note: The meat from a young sheep; compare with the animal.

items.example: He ordered pork with potatoes.
items.note: The meat from a pig.

items.example: We usually have chicken with rice.
items.note: Here chicken means the meat, not a live bird.

items.example: My sister is vegetarian, so she does not eat meat or fish.
items.note: A person who does not eat meat, including fish; also used as an adjective.

items.example: I baked salmon with lemon and herbs.
items.note: A type of fish; the letter l is silent in pronunciation.

items.example: The restaurant serves prawns with garlic.
items.note: British English term for these small shellfish; American usage often prefers shrimp.

items.example: The mussels were cooked in a tomato sauce.
items.note: Shellfish with two dark shells; pronounced like muscles.

items.example: They ordered fresh crab by the sea.
items.note: A sea animal with a hard shell and claws.

items.example: This restaurant is famous for its seafood.
items.note: Food from the sea, especially shellfish and also fish.

items.example: You can eat the skin of this pear.
items.note: The outer covering of some fruits; compare peel and rind.
